POS product tile — the Poster, full spectrum

Chosen 2026-10-12 from the four-direction board. The picture is the whole tile and the words sit on a scrim at its foot: the card colour (white in light, near-black in dark) at 85 %, eased over 48 px above the words, then flat under them; decided 2026-10-12. This board is every kind of tile, every state, and every one of the nine fields the store can switch on, alone and together. Nothing is removed: SKU, barcode, categories, tax and cost stay as options, each with a fixed home, because a store that wants cost on the tile is the point of a configurable POS. The Fields switches in the strip drive every frame except the fixed recipe rows.

The tile

The picture is the whole tile; the words sit on a scrim at its foot and the scrim grows only as far as the words need. Every tile in the grid is the same square whatever the store switches on, so the grid never ragged-edges and six fields on one tile never pushes its neighbours. Shown here with all nine fields on.

  1. Corners carry marks, never sentences. Top-left: the stock count (amber under the low-stock threshold, a clock for backorder, nothing when the product does not manage stock). Top-right: how many are in the cart, and on the parent tile the way back. A category: the folder glyph.
  2. Name. Two lines, then clipped. A variation shows the parent's name small and its options as chips, so no tile ever reads as a product called "Blue".
  3. Money row. Price, then the Sale pill and the struck regular price, then the tax line, wrapping as a row, never a stack. "from" before a variable product's range. Sold out replaces the price, and the picture greys: one message, not two.
  4. Facts. Cost, SKU, barcode, categories: label and value pairs that flow and wrap, so one fact is one short line and six are three. A store that cares about cost puts Cost first; it is the first fact.
  5. The scrim is the card colour, eased. White in light mode, near-black in dark, at 85 %; the fade is an eased curve over the 48 px above the first line and a flat plateau under the words, so a two-line tile and a seven-line tile fade identically. On a white product shot the scrim vanishes into the shot and the tile reads as a captioned picture; a dark photo gets a soft light foot.
  6. No picture is a tint, not a grey box. The tint comes from the product's first category (the same six light/dark pairs the categories use), so a shelf of services reads as one family. A category without a photo is its name set large on its tint, or a mosaic of its products (the one open choice, below).

The nine fields, your switches

The Fields switches in the strip turn each field on and off on every frame below. Only name and price are on by default in the app; the rest are the store's choice. This frame is a store with photos; the next has none, because a scrim with nothing under it is the test the tint has to pass.

Field recipes

Fixed rows that ignore the switches: what the same eight tiles look like for stores that set the panel up differently. The point is that each is a design, not a degraded version of the full one.

Every kind

What tells a product from a category from a variable product from a variation, on the Poster: the folder glyph and the count on a category; the stack and "N options" on a variable product; chips under a small parent name on a variation; the way-back badge on whichever tile sits in slot 0.

In the grid

The three places the cashier stands: the root, inside a category, inside a variable product. Same switches, same columns.

Where a tile design usually breaks. Switch Fields to everything and Columns to 6 and Phone on this one.

The one open choice: a category with no photo

Both keep the Poster's shape. The tint needs nothing from the data; the mosaic needs the category's first four product pictures, which the browse source does not fetch today.

What the category leaders do

Official help centres, developer docs and vendor source, read 2026-10-12 (the full survey with fifty sources is in the research note beside this file). Mobbin was queried too: it indexes Square's dashboard and Fresha's checkout but no POS register grid; the consumer grocery grids there (Talabat, Careem, foodpanda, Gojek) all agree with the table below.

What four or more of them agree on

  • Colour is the no-photo fallback, chosen by the merchant everywhere but Clover; Square adds a two-letter abbreviation. Woo has no colour field, so ours has to be derived (here: from the category) and still look chosen.
  • The photo is the tile; the words are a strip. Shopify uses it as the background; Square, Lightspeed and Odoo crop it on top with a name strip under. Nobody draws a padded thumbnail inside a card.
  • Stock on the tile is a number, never a phrase. Square and Toast print the count; Toast and Clover grey the tile and show a zero when gone. Low stock is a notification, not a badge.
  • The parent tile opens a chooser. Square and Lightspeed also let the merchant pin a single variation as its own tile. Nobody prints a "from" range on the tile.
  • Category tiles are the product tile's shape, told apart by colour and by what happens on tap. Only Odoo moves them out of the grid into a bar. Which is exactly the confusion you named; the leaders live with it because their tiles are merchant-placed, so the cashier already knows the layout. Ours are generated from the catalogue, so the shape has to say it.
  • Nothing beyond name, price and stock lives on the tile. SKU, barcode, category, tax, cost and strike-through prices live in item detail in all ten. We keep them as options (the shipped app has them), so the job is to give them one quiet home, not a row each.

Worth stealing

  • Odoo's in-cart numeral on the card and its category tint inherited by products: a grid that reads by colour family with no per-item setup (Direction D).
  • Toast's light/dark colour pairs: every tint here is defined twice, once per theme.
  • Square's abbreviation on colour, with the known complaint that "IN / IN / IN" collides; the mosaic of a category's own products avoids the collision for categories entirely.
  • Toast's one rule for stock: the count when there is one, greyed with a zero when there is none.

Rules this board keeps

  • Never colour alone: the low-stock pill carries the number, sold out carries the word, the folder carries the tab.
  • No kind label on every tile ("Category", "Variable"): the shape says it.
  • Tiles stay equal width in fixed columns; no tile grows a row because a field was switched on.
  • Tabular numerals on every amount and count; nothing under 12 px.
  • Semantic tokens only; the tints are six light/dark pairs added to the theme, named by hue, not by category.
